articles.title: Long Live the Prom Queen: Carrie Is Back and Mike Flanagan Has Successfully Made the Case for Why Her Story Needed to Be Retold
articles.summary: Review: With smart story accommodations for the social media age and a pair of stellar performances from Summer H. Howell and Samantha Sloyan, Mike Flanagan and his team have successfully made the case for why Carrie’s story needed to be retold.
articles.body:
Carrie debuts on Prime Video on October 7 . This is a spoiler-free review.

It’s easy to forget that for all the haunted hotels, dark towers, cursed cemeteries, society-ending viruses, killer clowns, and various and sundry things that go bump in the night that Stephen King has subjected us to, the author’s half-century grip on the horror genre started with a telekinetic teenage girl named Carrie White. Carrie’s cautionary tale of bullying has been adapted and sequelized numerous times, and Kimberly Peirce’s 2013 film even beat Mike Flanagan to the punch by first pulling Carrie into the 21st century. But, as is often the case when Flanagan brings King to the screen, Carrie successfully celebrates what makes the novel so relevant 52 years after its first publication by evolving with the times and palpably deepening King’s characters.

The opening moments of the premiere treat Carrie’s story with a Shakespearean level of reverence, with a Greek chorus of doc-style talking heads giving an overview of the story’s well-known beats that led to that fateful prom night. Inviting a closer look at all angles of that story is the dramatic thrust of Carrie, and the series sets itself up well for that effort by structuring itself as a teen drama in the vein of Pretty Little Liars or Riverdale. Carrie is an epistolary novel which heavily relies on interviews with the survivors of the prom night massacre and documentary evidence to tell Carrie’s story, and the series replicates that fractured perspective of the events by quickly setting up different groups of characters tied to Carrie as focal points for the narrative to jump around to.

Flanagan and his team are broadly successful in adapting the story and themes already present in King’s novel to the teen drama format. Carrie’s not a plot-heavy book, and the series compensates for that by spending more time on exploring how everyone is processing the events as they play out, and how the evolving interpersonal and public relations crises are picking at scabs at the back of the minds of characters like Carrie’s teacher Rita Desjardin (Amber Midthunder) and Principal Grayle (Matthew Lillard). The extra time and scope afforded to the story is a rising tide that lifts all boats, even if that format does occasionally leave room for some overwrought stylistic or dramatic choices. There are a few too many on-the-nose dream pop needle drops with lyrics that explain what the action of a given scene has already communicated just fine.

Carrie is not one of Stephen King’s strongest characters on the page - that epistolary style of the novel leaves Carrie often feeling a little decentralized from her own story - but that problem doesn’t persist into the TV series. The Carrie series is unquestionably successful in its most important effort: putting the plight of its two central characters, Carrie and Margaret White, into a modern context. As Carrie, Summer H. Howell is totally magnetic from her first moments onscreen. Carrie’s wide-eyed enthusiasm for integrating with the outside world is contagious, even as her first day with classmates like good-natured Sue Snell (Siena Agudong) and mean girl Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton) proves to be overwhelming. Howell’s accommodating and empathetic energy, even in the face of how poorly Carrie’s treated by the world, is a well of positivity and light that Flanagan and his team of directors - Kate Siegel, Axelle Carolyn, Kyra Sedgwick and Hiromi Kamata - continually put to the test across not just the classic challenges from her story, but the new ones afforded by the present-day setting. As Carrie becomes more self-assertive and is then tempted towards darkness, Howell’s work is even more impressive, and the writing does a good job giving her the space to take Carrie down more intense lanes without losing sight of the precocious girl she is at heart.

Carrie getting pelted with tampons in the shower by a gang of girls led by Regina George Chris Hargensen while she gets her first period is bad enough, but the show follows that event to its next logical permutation in 2026: what happens when video of that kind of horrific bullying makes its way onto social media in the form of a meme account run by Chris, “CarrieRed.” The viral spread of the “CarrieRed” account, and the resulting fallout, is a reliable kettle the show keeps on the boil throughout the season. With that in mind, despite its supernatural trappings, much of the show’s horror is internal and existential. There are surely scares, but by and large, Carrie is content to let the experience of being a teenage girl be its own engine of horror.

Of course, Carrie’s reaction to being so callously treated by people she just wanted to be friends with is paramount, but the show takes pains to keep Sue and Chris’s experiences of these in focus as the two social poles between which Carrie is being pulled. Both Siena Agudong and Alison Thornton are good in their roles, but with Sue being a naturally decent person who usually makes the right decision, it’s Thornton’s volatile Chris that winds up with more exciting material, especially given how Flanagan and company use her own complicated circumstances at home to serve as a foil to Carrie’s. Chris’ life is falling apart, with an estranged mom and a jerk father whose poor planning leaves her freshman year of college in jeopardy, and despite the fathomless cruelty that Chris inflicts on Carrie, the writing finds grace for Chris by making clear that there are plenty of ways that poor parenting can leave a girl ill-equipped to navigate the trials of growing up in 2026.

Carrie’s relationship to the events of the plot are largely unchanged from the novel, so it’s Samantha Sloyan’s Margaret White, Carrie’s mother, who winds up as the character with the most worthwhile overhaul here. Margaret White is one of the most famous religious zealots of horror fiction, but this series explores the roots of that fundamentalism in a much more nuanced way, a mission statement the series makes right off the bat with a canny alteration to the book’s inciting incident.

The death of Ralph White, Margaret’s husband, still leads to the authorities discovering Carrie’s shut-in conditions back at home but, this time, the cops discover both Carrie and Margaret holed up in the family prayer closet, where sinners in this house are sent to repent. The way Ralph looms as a specter over their home even after his death makes it clear as the season continues that Margaret’s fervent attempts at protecting her daughter from the outside world are rooted in the ways her relationship to her ultra-right wing husband warped her own worldview. Margaret sees herself as a holy warrior, and is there no more ungodly battlefield in that war than the town square of social media, especially with her daughter being savaged there on a daily basis?

Samantha Sloyan, a frequent Flanagan collaborator, is perfectly cast as Margaret, with the actress’s intensity and openness each a perfect fit for the character’s megalomania and genuine love for Carrie. Sloyan is at her best taking that holy warrior energy toe-to-toe with those she sees as adversaries at the school, like Principal Grayle, who are mostly doing their best to balance doing right by Carrie with the institutional loopholes that leave them hamstrung in those efforts. How willing others in the town of Chamberlain seem to be to cosign Margaret’s style of guardianship call attention to her pridefulness in ways that don’t let her off the hook from being responsible for her choices, but do wonders for pointing out how prevalent the tendency to be “holier than thou” really is these days.

What shakiness is present in how Carrie is expanded out to eight episodes of TV comes from a side plot and characters that Flanagan and the writers have created to underline Carrie’s significance to the wider Kingverse. Their presence does at least make sense, given how freely the Carrie novel acknowledges the presence of other characters with the “TK gene” out in the world. Flanagan uses one character in particular to give structure to each episode, most beginning with her narration about the story of another gifted girl or woman out in the world. It’s during these vignettes that the series’ writing is at its least subtle, lacking enough variety in how they speak to the way Carrie represents all disenfranchised women to keep them from feeling a little repetitious by the season’s end.

The varying mileage these additional plot elements get is perhaps best represented in the presence of another brand-new character, Emaline (Thalia Dudek). Emaline is another new student at Ewen High who befriends Carrie and encourages her to take a more active stance against her antagonists but, as written, Emaline’s function in the story winds up being a little too one-note for a little too long to feel like a necessary invention. The Carrie series folds in this supporting roster of characters sparingly, but their presence does call for the show’s focus to occasionally drift, especially as things start heating up going into the finale.

articles.title: South Park Season 29 Skewers the Wealthy Elite in "Billionaire Weenietown," but It's Butters Who Steals the Show
articles.summary: South Park Season 29's second episode doesn't fully click, but you can always count on Butters and his dysfunctional family to carry the day.
articles.body:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for South Park Season 29, Episode 2!

Following a season premiere that felt like a throwback to a more classic incarnation of South Park , the series pivots in Episode 2 with a more topical approach. As the title suggests, "Billionaire Weenietown" is all about skewering the billionaire class, specifically the fact that we can't seem to escape their attention-seeking, data center-building ways. It's a fine episode, but one that's mostly carried by the ever-dependable Butters and his family.

The conflict this week comes as Butters finds he can no longer enjoy his precious Dr. Pimple Popper videos. South Park America has become infested with billionaires who have built a power-hungry new data center literally in Butters' backyard. And he's not going to stand for it one minute longer.

Again, I think the Stotch family storyline in this episode works a bit better than the Weenietown half of things. There's certainly a fun novelty in seeing just how literally this episode takes the whole "Billionaire Weenietown" concept. There's never not some fun to be had in watching a bunch of talking penises bicker with each other and go on The Joe Rogan Experience. It's a way for the series to make fun of the Elon Musks and Mark Zuckerbergs of the world without directly including them.

But as is sometimes the case on this show, the shelf life of that particular gag is limited. This episode leans a bit too hard on the "billionaires are dorks who think everyone wants to hear their opinions" joke when, frankly, there are a lot more reasons to make fun of them besides. The resolution to the Weenietown conflict is also a bit too simple and abrupt for my liking. That said, I'm curious to see if the writers find ways of integrating the remaining Billionaire Weenies into the remainder of Season 29. Hopefully they don't become the new Member Berries...

But it's hard to muster too much criticism for an episode that gives us such a concentrated dose of Butters. If anything, this normally plucky, innocent character is even more entertaining when he's pushed over the edge. Angry Butters is a good Butters, and that anger really carries the day here. Whether it's his tantrum in the classroom or his interactions with the pest control guy, Butters is a real hoot here. Who can't empathize with his righteous anger at this point?

Well, his parents sure can't. Butters' crusade tees up a hilarious subplot where Steve and Linda Stotch fear their precious baby boy has contracted "libtardedness." That subplot serves as a terrific sendup of the anti-vax movement and a certain brand of self-educated, Joe Rogan-loving know-it-all. With the two parents having a complete meltdown while Butters is off doing his own thing, this episode feels like a direct callback to 2001's "Butters' Very Own Episode." That formula still works very well. Though this subplot does sort of drop off before the end. I was expecting some sort of payoff to the FBI call that never comes. Maybe that's a seed for another day?

Finally, I can't not mention the ending. After going nearly two full episodes without roasting Donald Trump directly, the series turns all of its wrath back his way with another goofy deepfake sequence. It's an amusing way to cap off this episode. Coming off of such a Trump-heavy Season 27 and 28, I wouldn't necessarily mind if the show limited itself to these occasional roasts rather than making him a central character again. We'll just have to see what direction Season 29 takes as we get closer to November and the all-important release of GTA.

articles.title: Dracula: Book IV - The Undead Concludes an Epic Vampire Saga
articles.summary: We've got an exclusive preview of Dracula: Book IV - The Undead, as Matt Wagner and Kelley Jones' landmark vampire saga comes to a close.
articles.body:
The appeal with Matt Wagner and Kelley Jones' Dracula graphic novels has always been clear. Two legendary creators joining forces to put a fresh spin on the unnaturally long life of Dracula? Sign us up. But all good things must come to an end. Wagner and Jones are teaming up one last time to wrap up their vampire saga in Dracula: Book IV - The Undead.

With the Kickstarter campaign for Dracula: Book IV - The Undead live now, IGN can exclusively debut the first five pages of this graphic novel. Check them out in the slideshow gallery below:

Dracula: Book IV - The Undead Preview Gallery

As with the previous volumes, Dracula: Book IV is written by Wagner and illustrated by Jones, with both providing cover art. The book is published through their Orlok Press label and, based on the first three volumes, will likely later be released in bookstores via Dark Horse Comics.

Dracula: Book IV - The Undead is set after the events of Bram Stoker's original novel. It turns out that Jonathan Harker and his allies weren't quite thorough enough in dispatching their foe, allowing Dracula to rise from the grave and threaten the world once more.

“In the novel, Professor Van Helsing outlines very clearly how to destroy a vampire,” said Wagner in a statement. "And yet, in the exciting climax of the story, the British heroes don’t really use those prescribed methods to attack their foe. That discrepancy, combined with the fact that the sun is just about to set and thus restore Dracula to the full extent of his vampiric powers has provided us with the perfect opportunity to explore beyond the events of the original novel.”

“As always, I’m continually blown away by Kelley’s incredible art for these tales,” added Wagner. “I’m distinctly writing this saga with his graphic prowess always in mind…and yet he somehow always seems to draw each scene and moment even better than I had imagined. If Dracula did, indeed, survive the events of the original novel, what would be his response to the human enemies who so very nearly managed to end his centuries of evil dominion? Can anyone resist the vampire lord’s unholy vengeance? If their victory over his evil was only imaginary, then Dracula is truly…THE UNDEAD!”

The Kickstarter campaign for Dracula: Book IV - The Undead is live now. You can also find Amazon links to order the previous three volumes below:

articles.title: March of Giants Might Actually Get You to Play a MOBA Besides Dota 2 and League | IGN Preview
articles.summary: It's wild to challenge the titans of it like League of Legends and Dota 2. However, key developers on March of Giants also worked on another game you'd think was challenging immovable competition—Rainbow Six Siege, which in many ways went up against tactical shooter titan Counter-Strike and has survived and thrived to this day. From what I saw, March of Giants is playing some of the same cards as Siege did, including one key decision: While it plans to incorporate the accessibility you expect from a game made in this decade, March of Giants doesn't dilute the genre. It has the hardcore things that have survived and thrived in the MOBA for years—from big stuff like separate skill leveling and complex itemization to the littler things like last hitting.
articles.body:
March of Giants shakes up the somewhat-rigid MOBA genre in a compelling way.

Strategies aplenty here; you’ve got plenty of options for how to achieve victory.

Two opposing armies seek to lay low their enemies' lines of fortifications, outlying outposts, and supply depots. They rely on coordinated pushes, often suicidal assaults for the many troops involved, to break their enemies' will. They seek to develop or acquire new strategies and technologies to break the stalemate of fighting over an ever-growing no man's land. I'm either describing Trench Warfare or the very popular MOBA genre, or, in the case of the upcoming March of Giants, both at the same time.

It's a MOBA that in the words of its lead designer wants to turn the arena into a battlefield. Players in the 4v4 matches are towering giants infused with mythical power who serve as champions and commanders for their side, shaping their three traditional lanes into a warfront with bastions of defense built up by the players—even pulling soldiers and supplies away to meet needs on another front.

I got to spend a day playing its current in-development build, and I think that it's looking surprisingly promising. I say surprising because the genre has historically been pretty set in stone. It's wild to challenge the titans of it like League of Legends and Dota 2. However, key developers on March of Giants also worked on another game you'd think was challenging immovable competition—Rainbow Six Siege, which in many ways went up against tactical shooter titan Counter-Strike and has survived and thrived to this day.

From what I saw, March of Giants is playing some of the same cards as Siege did, including one key decision: While it plans to incorporate the accessibility you expect from a game made in this decade, March of Giants doesn't dilute the genre. It has the hardcore things that have survived and thrived in the MOBA for years—from big stuff like separate skill leveling and complex itemization to the littler things like last hitting.

But it didn't feel tired. The big change is how the developers want the players to change and manipulate the battlefield. Commanding your retinue of soldiers is another ability in your arsenal as a player, as is placing battleworks that fortify positions and inevitably become ruins that shape the conflict's future.

In a typical match you can expect to contest a lane against one or more enemy heroes, all while trying to get experience points by taking out enemies and snatching up requisition points and supplies from the ruined city sections outside the attack lanes. The requisition is your money—used to upgrade your giant's own body. The supplies become battleworks, which can buy you an advantage in a pushed-forward lane or help your team hold on to a struggling one—a lot of which is down to what kind of hero you're playing and playing against. More on that later.

Battleworks aren't just defenses, either, but ironclad tanks, cavalry charges, and airship soldier drops. There's no RTS-style micro and basecraft going on here, but March of Giants is closer to the MOBA genre's RTS roots than I've felt a game has been in years. It reminds of the glory days of Warcraft 3 custom maps, where all kinds of wild ideas for what a MOBA could be were thought up and discarded.

As the match progresses you start to try and contest your enemy's supply depots and shop points, destroying them to empower your own team's abilities and deny enemies safe harbor. You also fight the opposing team over neutral objectives, like siege dozers that plow into enemy bunkers and towers like little else in the game. They're a perfect catalyst for a teamfight to kick off over, or for a lone sneaky hero to snap away from a distracted opposition. There's also bigger bosses to knock down—a vicious automated defense system and a rogue airship—that reward your team with big boosts to make strong pushes against the enemy, like a siege cannon that can reduce even end-game defenses to rubble.

To win, you just take out two of your enemy's three final citadels. It sounds easy, but the size of the March of Giants map is smaller than the map in other big-name MOBAs. You have breathing room, but once the match hits that 10- or 15-minute mark things start to get very claustrophobic—and any big game-winning push can have the entire enemy team there to defend it posthaste. And then it'll be over. March of Giants is designed to have its matches take roughly 20 to 30 minutes. I saw nothing longer than 25. I think you'll be able to get at least two, maybe three rounds played in an hour. It's a very appealing concept if you're fitting in gaming between other things. Of course, with the build freedom the developers are emphasizing, I could see a match that takes an extreme of 45 minutes or more.

The core of that flexibility is the characters. While many of them look like just another big dude, I'd encourage you to look deeper than the obvious ones on the art. There's also a skeleton. A werewolf. A tree. A cthulhu. A… whatever a Trench Maw is. Each character has a variety of builds: What order you get your skills while leveling, which items you buy, and eventually where you put the scarce augment points that boost your skills by making them longer ranged, able to shoot more projectiles, and a host of other stuff.

Iron Sister, for example, is a threatening mobile support character that can lay down some real damage, slow enemies, and anchor a defense. You could build that character into a strong support, laying out ability damage and team buffs and heals. You could also very easily build her skillset into an obnoxiously tanky menace that does her supporting from the middle of the enemy team. I didn't feel like the match or two I played as or against any given character even began to scratch the surface of what they could be built for.

I love this because it's playing into one of the best parts of a strong MOBA. Less is not more when it comes to character design, no: More is more. No single character is balanced against every other character: The ecosystem of characters as a whole is balanced. The game doesn't start when you spawn, it starts when you pick and counter-pick against the enemy team during the draft phase. That lets the developers embrace wackier out-there character designs like Trench Maw, who burrows around and spawns extra soldiers from the armored bunker on his back, or Dreadnought, whose entire toolkit revolves around locking down lanes with anti-titan bunkers that boost his skills.

While I must emphasize that March of Giants is definitely its own thing, it's a philosophy that reminds me more of Dota 2 than League of Legends, and that, I think, is a promising sign. From the way they spoke, the developers aren't going to put their foot on the scale and limit the freedom of what you can build a character into—but if you discover a wild new combo they're more likely to find out how to buff its counterplays than nerf it.

The new thing in March of Giants—and the thing I expect to see some insane community strategies come out of—are of course the systems for commanding soldiers and building battleworks. Your squad of soldiers is commanded with just two keys. One to send them out in a straight line or redirect their path mid-charge, another to recall them. With that simple system you can use your soldiers to do all manner of stuff. You can send them to gather supplies or money for you. You can break off small parties of them to serve as scouts, checking a spot of woods or ruined buildings for concealed enemies. You need soldiers to break open the defensive shields that allow enemy towers and bunkers to be damaged, and a charge of soldiers is also the most fearsome damage source against enemy giants! Indeed, swarming soldiers deal their own entire, unresistable damage type separate from attacks and ability damage.

Of course, Giants aren't defenseless. You can autoattack larger targets like guns and armored cars. But soldiers are too small to be targeted. Instead, you just left click to stomp. And watching the hundreds of soldiers dance around the screen didn't get old during the time I had to play. In fact, I felt like I was barely scratching the surface of an unexplored, complex new game system. Props to the March of Giants team for that.

That's not even to mention the Giants that change how their soldiers behave or give them buffs. Wolfgang's soldiers turn into a horde of ravenous werewolves, while Voidmaster turns them into tentacular cultists, and Ossuary turns his into a horde of ghosts who can pass through walls—hilarious for stealing supplies out from under the enemy's nose!

The real counter to soldiers is… your own side's soldiers and your battlework defenses. Laying out trenches stops charges cold, or at least slows them down. Anti-giant bunkers mean your enemy can't get close to follow up on a charge they sent in. And both of those are countered by hard pushes with ironclad tanks or cavalry charges. Like real trench warfare, however, you can't fight over the same ground forever. The ruins of buildings prevent things from being built in the same spot later on—a devastated no man's land that emerges naturally as the teams push back and forth through each others' lines of defense.

It keeps the matches snappy and prevents them from becoming stalemates.It's a nice parallel to March of Giants themes as a whole. You're at the peak of this industrial fantasy world's trench warfare—and the Giants are here to break it all down. More is more, baby.

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!

Jon Bolding is a regular contributor to IGN who does most of his gaming on PC. Talk PC gaming with him on X/Twitter at @JonBolds .

articles.title: Can VR glasses save VR?
articles.summary: Meta VR Glasses might make more sense than headsets — not just because of size and weight, but due to passthrough vision, peripheral vision, and field of view.
articles.body: I’m pretty sure I won’t be buying the $1,299 Meta VR Glasses. That’s too rich for my blood in today’s economy, and my feelings about Meta are… conflicted. But I want you to understand that Meta just changed the game. We’ve had glasses, but we’ve never had glasses like this. The Meta VR Glasses are not an opaque VR headset. They are not a pair of transparent AR glasses. They might be the best of both. After playing with the Meta VR Glasses, Valve’s Steam Frame, the Apple Vision Pro, and the Google / Xreal Aura back to back, I think they’re the first design that could convince regular people to give VR a chance. It’s not because they look like glasses. It’s not just that they’re five times lighter than a typical headset at around 100 grams. It’s certainly not the $1,300 price tag, even if that’s much less than a $3,700 Vision Pro. It’s about what you see and feel — and what you don’t see and feel — when you put Meta’s VR Glasses on your head. You aren’t fully enclosed. You aren’t isolated. Because the Meta VR Glasses are glasses, not goggles, you have real peripheral vision. You see a live video feed of your room in the center, thick “rims” around that, then an actual naked-eye view of your surroundings around those rims. Even when you’re in a game, you still have peripheral vision. I know people who aren’t comfortable in VR at home because they can’t afford to feel isolated from their kids or pets. I’ve personally never felt comfortable wearing headsets on a plane or train or in a park because I don’t like being surrounded by strangers I can’t easily see. Women have told me VR is a nonstarter because they have long hair or wear makeup. Many headsets balance their weight by sandwiching your head between a back strap and a front cushion, and they don’t want to deal with the hassle of a high ponytail or smears every time they strap in. Glasses are a potential solution, resting on your ears and floating before your eyes instead of pushing on your head. For years, the industry has suggested headsets will eventually make way for glasses. But typically when we talk about glasses, they’re transparent. We’re imagining indistinguishable-from-eyeglasses spectacles that let you see the real world in all its glory, then magically make virtual objects appear within the entirety of the frame. Today’s transparent-display glasses have made leaps and bounds, but they’re not there yet. While the basic lenses might look like glasses and give you a glasses-like field of view, the displays inside the glasses light up a much smaller area. When I sweep my head left or right, up or down, I see virtual objects disappear even when I’m still looking roughly in their direction. In 2013, I briefly wore Google Glass — a tiny screen above my right eye with a postage stamp-sized 15-degree diagonal field of view. In 2015, I tried Microsoft’s HoloLens, with a 34-degree field of view. Four years later, HoloLens 2 achieved 52 degrees diagonally, the Xreal One Pro glasses I’ve been testing offer 57 degrees, and the Xreal Aura will finally push transparent glasses to 70 degrees diagonal this fall. [Image: Oh look, it’s me from 2013. Guy had no idea what he was getting into. But even with the Aura, 70 degrees diagonal is more like 60 degrees horizontal by 40 degrees vertical. Humans have roughly 120 degrees of binocular vision alone, and VR headsets like the Meta Quest 3 and Steam Frame offer around 110 degrees horizontal so you can feel like a virtual world is all around you. Transparent glasses are also, well, transparent. Glasses like the Aura have to make their projected light compete with the real world while still letting you see through. That often means projectors right up against your brow. Virtual objects can seem ghostly unless you activate electrochromic lenses, which turn the clear lenses dark at the push of a button, blocking your view of the world. Even then, you can see games, movies, and virtual desktops far better in a VR headset, where virtual light and real light don’t have to compete. You see the real world through what’s called “passthrough vision” — a live camera feed — with virtual objects realistically appearing at the correct depth and blocking real-life objects behind them. [Image: The Steam Frame is one of the smallest, lightest, and most comfortable standalone VR headsets, but it’s still goggles. That’s how the Steam Frame, Meta Quest, and Apple Vision Pro all work. But again, they weigh four to eight times as much and are fully enclosed. What if there were a lighter, open-air set of glasses that used passthrough vision instead of transparent lenses? You see where I’m going with this. Instead of 60 degrees horizontal by 40 degrees vertical, the Meta VR Glasses offer 70 degrees by 66 degrees, and let me tell you, it feels like a bigger difference than it sounds. But the difference isn’t just the raw field of view — it’s that my real and virtual fields of view are the same. Anywhere I look inside the lenses, virtual objects can fill that frame, instead of getting abruptly cut off where the display part of the transparent display ends. It also doesn’t hurt that the VR Glasses offer much higher angular resolution than most AR or VR devices (37ppd), making it easier to read text. What you don’t get at 70 degrees by 66 degrees is full immersion. Some nerds like me will argue that the Meta VR Glasses don’t offer true VR, because it’s hard to feel like you’re “there” if you see so much less of your game. But it didn’t feel like I had tunnel vision, either, and it helps that the headset can track your hands far outside your field of view. Wearing the Meta VR Glasses was the first time I thought to myself: Is there such a thing as “enough” field of view? I’ll always want more, but maybe the problem with virtual reality isn’t about feeling immersed. The industry’s problem is convincing enough people that it’s worth wearing any sort of headgear at all. The 1-pound Steam Frame was a step in the right direction, but it’s still just for obsessives like me. Quarter-pound VR glasses that let you see your real world clearly will be a much easier sell. Even if you don’t plan to buy a $1,300 set from Meta, I suspect other companies are about to copy Meta’s homework. When it announced the VR Glasses, Meta called it “a new era for virtual reality,” and in an interview, VP of wearables Alex Himel told my colleague Victoria Song that “the future of everything we’re doing is a pair of augmented reality glasses.” As of February, it sounded like more goggles were still coming from Meta — but if the VR Glasses do well, I wouldn’t be surprised if it stops making headsets in the future.

articles.title: GTA 6 Gets Official ESRB Rating and It's as Mature as You'd Expect
articles.summary: In the most obvious turn of events, GTA 6 has officially been rated M for Mature by the ESRB, and it will of course include nudity.
articles.body:
In the most obvious turn of events, GTA 6 has officially been rated M for Mature by the ESRB, and it will of course include nudity.

Rockstar has added the official ratings for GTA 6 to the various store pages for the game, giving us some insight into what we can expect. If you've ever played a GTA game (or really, any major Rockstar game that isn't Bully or Midnight Club), you'll know that no stone is left unturned when it comes to adult content. There's sex, violence, drugs, alcohol, crime, and an excessive amount of coarse language. GTA 6 will continue that trend, as the game has been rated for "blood and gore, intense violence, mature humor, nudity, strong language, strong sexual content, use of drugs and alcohol."

The UK equivalent of the ESRB, PEGI, has issued a similar rating of PEGI 18. We're still waiting for the ESRB to post its more in-depth breakdown, which often provides specific references to scenes and content in games alongside its more general description. Those breakdowns hint at certain story elements and gameplay mechanics, so we may hear more about the kinds of sexual content and the level of violence when that becomes available. Fans have been speculating about whether or not Jason and Lucia will have sex on-screen in GTA 6, for example, so it's possible that the ESRB's detailed breakdown will confirm or squash that speculation.

Rockstar previously got into trouble back in the mid-2000s with the release of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, as the game had an interactive sex mini-game buried in its files. The mini-game was cut from the final game, but modders were able to add it back in. As a result of the "pornographic" content, the ESRB re-rated the game to an AO rating, effectively banning it from retailers. This led to a brief recall of the game and scrutiny from government officials.

Still, sexual content has found its way into GTA titles in the years since. GTA 4 and 5 allowed players to pick up sex workers and have intercourse with them in their vehicle. The player had minimal input on how this played out, but it certainly pushed buttons and created its own controversy. As of right now, it's unclear what kind of sexual content will be in GTA 6 beyond visiting strip clubs .

Additionally, the ESRB rating makes mention of "in-game purchases." Rockstar stated earlier this summer that there are "no monetizations in this game," which suggests there are no microtransactions. However, this likely refers to an upgrade from the standard edition of the game to the Ultimate Edition, which will give players access to additional cosmetics, stores, and missions. As of right now, Rockstar hasn't said a word about GTA 6's online mode, but it's not currently expected to launch alongside the game this year.

Presumably, the online mode will be monetized, just like its predecessor. In GTA 5, players can buy in-game currency to purchase clothing, vehicles, and properties. Given how much money GTA Online has generated for Rockstar over the years, it's hard to imagine the new online mode lacking microtransactions when it launches in the future. Currently, the online portion is rumored and speculated to debut in 2027 .

GTA 6 is now in its final push toward release, as there is less than 50 days until launch. Rockstar has put up signange in Miami to promote the game , sent out swag boxes to influencers, and announced a massive $400 collector's set , though the latter attracted controversy for not including a copy of the game .

We've got extensive coverage of GTA 6 across IGN. Check out IGN's interview with Rockstar Games , our GTA 6 preview , and word of the first confirmed GTA 6 voice actor .

articles.title: 007 First Light's First DLC Out Now, Adds New Game Plus
articles.summary: The 007 First Light Extended Operations DLC launches for free today, and adds five different missions to the TacSim mode, along with New Game Plus, new outfits and a photo mode that was somehow missing from the game at launch.
articles.body:
007 First Light launched earlier this year with the promise of future content being added to the TacSim mode, and IO Interactive has finally followed through.

The 007 First Light Extended Operations DLC launches for free today, and adds five different missions to the TacSim mode, along with New Game Plus, new outfits and a photo mode that was somehow missing from the game at launch.

Four of the new operations will revolve around the Valhalla, the supercar you get to play with in the campaign, like, once. According to the trailer, these Valhalla missions look like driving trials, where you'll use the car's weapons and gadgets to complete challenges on a timer. Unfortunately, you won't be able to just substitute it into other missions where you have to drive decidedly less exciting vehicles – at least not yet.

IO Interactive also added a New Game Plus mode, and that's probably what I'm going to be diving into first, especially with the path tracing update that came out a couple weeks ago . The mode also bring along a new 00 difficulty, which is supposedly significantly harder than the Purist difficulty in the original game. Enemies are going to react faster, some NPCs are swapped for more difficult variants, and combat is going to be way more unforgiving with two-hit kills and a tighter parry window.

Beyond the content additions, though, IO Interactive is also improving weapon animations and enemies will now be able to throw you off of a cliff, just like you were able to do to them in the base game. It's only fair, after all.

This is the first content-based DLC for 007 First Light and is a welcome return for one of the best games of the year so far. IGN's 007 First Light review returned a 9/10. We said: "Demonstrably obsessed with bringing the Bond fantasy to life in a way no one has ever managed before, 007 First Light is the best Bond game I’ve ever played."

While I'm sure some folks were hoping for a story expansion, the Extended Operations is free, and should tide people over before James Bond goes on any more official adventures. Hopefully the game will finally come out on Switch 2 next.

articles.title: Sony Finally Brings AI Upscaling To Base PS5
articles.summary: AI upscaling continues to be a huge part of the modern graphics pipeline, and while PSSR brought this tech to the PS5 Pro, the base PS5 was left without it due to its weaker GPU. That's been remedied, though, with QSSR.
articles.body:
AI upscaling continues to be a huge part of the modern graphics pipeline, and while PSSR brought this tech to the PS5 Pro, the base PS5 was left without it due to its weaker GPU. That's been remedied with QSSR.

In a blog post , Sony detailed a new upscaling model that runs on its base console called Quick Spectral Super Resolution, or QSSR. Just like the PSSR that debuted earlier this year on the PS5 Pro, QSSR was born from the Project Amethyst collaboration with AMD that kicked off last year.

The new model is much more lightweight than PSSR, and so it won't be quite as good at maintaining detail as PSSR is on the PS5 Pro, but it should be much more accurate than the temporal upscaling traditionally used on the console.

QSSR debuts in Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei, and the respective developers seem pretty enthused about working the technology into their games. Sony's blog quotes Insomniac Head of Technology Mike Fitzgerald, who said, "QSSR adds more pixel-level clarity and stability to our environments, bringing out extra detail amidst the busy streets of Madripoor, the dense alleyways of Shinjuku, and many other areas across Logan’s epic journey. It’s a perfect companion to the launch of Marvel’s Wolverine, and it brings a great taste of the PS5 Pro experience to our players on PS5."

Likewise, Jasmin Patry, the Lead Rendering Engineer at Sucker Punch, said: “At Sucker Punch, we’re excited to bring QSSR to Ghost of Yōtei players so that they can experience the world we’ve created with even more clarity and detail. QSSR excels at resolving the fine details in our characters and environments and does so with a level of temporal stability that hasn’t been possible on the PS5 console until now. We’ve long wished that all PS5 players could experience the incredible image quality that PSSR brings to PS5 Pro, and QSSR is a positive step towards that goal!”

The blog also shared a couple of clips from the respective games showing QSSR in action, compared to the standard temporal upscaling on the base PS5, and the results are promising. In Wolverine, the clip zooms in on distant buildings, and while the QSSR sample is still quite blurry – it is a watered down model, after all – it is able to maintain a lot more detail in fine objects than the standard clip on the left.

Then, in Ghost of Yotei, the camera zooms in on foliage in the foreground. In the original PS5 sample, the grass is almost a collection of floating green lines, with aliasing that cuts it up into sections. With QSSR enabled, the grass maintains its actual shape, even if it's still a bit noisy.

Obviously, the model running on the more powerful PS5 Pro is going to be better at maintaining image quality than QSSR ever will. But, the PS5 Pro will now set you back $900, and so this lighter model at least brings this upscaling to more people. Sony does say that it is making QSSR available to all developers, so I'd only expect more studios to use it going forward.

Still, we've only seen this model in action in a couple of clips on Sony's blog, so I'm not sure exactly how well it'll perform. Luckily, the patch for Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei will be going live later today, so I'll be able to see how well it holds up. But I do hope it works well, because QSSR could help bridge the gap for anyone who won't be able to afford a likely expensive PlayStation 6 for at least an extra few months.

articles.title: Sony brings AI graphics upscaling to the regular PS5
articles.summary: Sony’s new Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) for PS5 brings improvements to image detail and image stability. It’s being added to Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei.
articles.body: Sony is launching a new AI upscaling technology specifically for the regular PS5. The new tech, called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), is a “new performance tier of AI upscaling” that’s a result of Sony’s Project Amethyst work with AMD, according to a blog post. Sony says that PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), which is available on the PS5 Pro, “remains the gold standard,” and in Digital Foundry’s early hands-on with the tech, it does seem that QSSR isn’t as fast as PSSR because the PS5 doesn’t have dedicated machine learning silicon. As a result, you should probably expect closer to an upscaled 1440p resolution on PS5 instead of the upscaled 4K on PS5 Pro. ”On PS5 Pro, developers almost uniformly output to 4K and adjust render resolution beneath it,” Sony principal graphics R&D engineer Daniel Craig told Digital Foundry. “On PS5, teams have to be more flexible, tuning not just render resolution, but also their intermediate and final presentation targets depending on the graphics mode.” But Craig also said that QSSR is “fundamentally a drop-in replacement for titles that already support PSSR” after only a few days of tuning, making it likelier that PS5 developers will take advantage. The tech will be “offered broadly to all PlayStation developers,” Sony says. Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei will be the first games to take advantage of QSSR, and are getting patches today to offer the tech as “an additional graphics option on PS5.” (Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition also launches today.) Here are a couple videos from Sony showing off how QSSR looks in those games, and it appears to make graphics a little bit sharper: [Media: [Media: Digital Foundry writes that “the potential here is remarkable: low resolution and poor upscaling have impacted so many titles in this generation, but QSSR could make a big difference.”

articles.summary:

Director Marq Evans (“Claydream”) and producer Tamir Ardon (“Claydream,” “Skywalkers: A Love Story”) infuse this story of family and fabulists with a striking emotional heft, featuring never-before-seen archival footage and original interviews with figures both famous and infamous within the vibrant Bigfoot community. In whole, the doc amounts to the most momentous shake-up of the billion-dollar Bigfoot industry to hit the big screen since Patterson himself toured the nation with his proof of Patty.

articles.title: See Why Deicidium Returned Is One of 2026's Most Promising New Graphic Novels
articles.summary: The team behind DC's critically acclaimed New Gods relaunch are back with Deicidium Returned, and it's one of the most exciting new graphic novels of 2026.
articles.body:
DC's All In initiative has been responsible for some pretty great comics in the last couple of years, but it's tough to top Ram V and Evan Cagle's New Gods. Luckily, while that series only lasted 12 issues, the creators are reuniting for a new graphic novel called Deicidium Returned. That's enough to immediately make it one of our most anticipated books in the months ahead.

With the final order cutoff for Deicidium Returned happening on October 5, IGN can exclusively debut the first 24 pages of this graphic novel. Feast your eyes on this gorgeous comic bookery in the slideshow gallery below:

Image Comics' Deicidium Returned Preview Gallery

Decidium Returned is written by Ram V, with art by Evan Cagle and Anand Radhakrishnan. The book is published through Image Comics. Here's the official summary:

In a future rebuilt from the ashes of war, belief is no longer sacred—it’s monetized.

Humanity has entered a hard-won age of stability, governed by an unholy alliance between global corporations and newly engineered religions. Worship fuels the economy. Faith is power. Salvation is a product. Welcome to the industry of belief. That fragile balance shatters when the old gods return. Ancient deities of fire, wind, jaguars, love, war, and mischief awaken inside ordinary people, transforming neighbors and strangers into living gods. To the powers that be, they aren’t miracles—they’re threats.

The great faiths of the new world knew the old gods could one day return, and they planned for such an eventuality. 12 orphans were chosen, bestowed with gifts and taught to be faithless, loveless instruments without reward or remorse. The old gods have returned—and the 12 will be unleashed.

As old myths collide with a world built on manufactured faith, a brutal conflict ignites—one that will decide who controls humanity’s future, and whether salvation comes from those placed above us…or from within us. DEICIDIUM is a global epic series from the multi-award-winning collaborations of RAM V, EVAN CAGLE, ANAND RADHAKRISHNAN with TOM MULLER, ADITYA BIDIKAR and more.

"A daring heist. A pair of thieves in slums around a holy city. A biker gang of graverobbers around a mausoleum town. A protest at the foot of a sacred mountain. This is how DEICIDIUM begins," V tells IGN. "Separate threads, looking at the lives of ordinary, seemingly unconnected people in a world that is run by faith, worship and the commerce of belief. An explosive revelation is to follow. Something old was stolen. Something ancient is broken. Clever machiavellian fingers pulling at long-forgotten threads. What if these ordinary people with loves, lives and lingering regrets...what if these people were actually gods? Would we love them? Hate them? Hold them up or would we kill them?"

Deicidium Returned will be released on November 11. You can preorder a copy on Amazon .

articles.title: Steam Deck 2: Is AMD Gainsborough the chip Valve’s been waiting for?
articles.summary: AMD drivers have leaked the codename for a previously unknown chip: an “AMD Gainsborough.” Could it be the Steam Deck 2’s chip?
articles.body: The Steam Deck is four and a half years old, and handheld gamers are eagerly awaiting a Steam Deck 2 — but Valve has consistently said it needs a new chip with a “generational leap” in performance and efficiency before building the sequel. There’s some reason to believe that chip has now broken cover: AMD Gainsborough. But I’m a tad skeptical. As leaker Moore’s Law is Dead and IT Home report, the latest AMD drivers have leaked the codename for a previously unknown chip: an “AMD Gainsborough.” The first Steam Deck chip was named “Aerith” after Final Fantasy VII’s heartbreaking love interest, and Gainsborough is her last name. Plus, the chip appears to be a semi-custom one (read: designed for a specific customer) on TSMC’s relatively recent N3P process. [Media: IT Home checked import/export records and found that AMD’s already been shipping test equipment for the Gainsborough chip for validation, suggesting that a potential customer might already be testing to see if it’s suitable for their device. [Image: Those import records also show the Gainsborough chip will be fairly small, with an FF6 package measuring 25mm by 25mm. Today, leaker Gotou_3rd seemingly revealed that AMD’s next handheld chips, the Ryzen Z3 and Z3 Extreme, will also be 25mm by 25mm chips. Gotou also published a possible fragment of an AMD slide deck that suggests the Z3 is targeting 15 watts, the same power envelope as the Steam Deck and Steam Deck OLED: [Image: This isn’t quite enough to tie Gainsborough specifically to a Steam Deck 2, though. First, a semi-custom chip doesn’t always wind up in its originally intended gadget. It’s long been rumored that the Steam Deck’s own semi-custom chip wasn’t originally designed for the Steam Deck, but rather a Magic Leap headset, and that it was shopped around for tablets (including this canceled Microsoft tablet, the story goes) before Valve took advantage. There are portions of the original Steam Deck’s chip that went entirely unused. Second, you should know that “Aerith” (Steam Deck), “Sephiroth” (Steam Deck OLED) and “Gainsborough” are not Valve’s codenames. When I visited Valve’s headquarters in late 2023, I commented on this Aerith wafer hanging on the wall — and Valve designers told me they didn’t really want the Final Fantasy codenames. AMD was the one that chose them. [Image: The Aerith wafer I saw at Valve HQ. Some extra evidence that Valve isn’t tied to those names: When Microsoft and Asus picked the “Ryzen Z2 A” chip for the vanilla $500 Xbox Ally, they were choosing an “Aerith Plus” chip. Third, 25mm by 25mm might be small, but it’s actually large for a Steam Deck! The original Steam Deck’s “Aerith” chip, before it shrunk to remove the unused components in its “Sephiroth” revision, reportedly measured 19mm by 19mm. But perhaps it’s efficient, and perhaps it’s more affordable if this apple doesn’t fall too far from AMD’s 25mm x 25mm Ryzen Z3 tree. Lastly, Valve was still figuring out “how and when” to do a Steam Deck 2 as of last month, after it would have theoretically received these Gainsborough chips. But I guess Valve might just be trying not to overpromise, after this year’s RAM-forced hardware delays.

articles.title: Ahead of Metro 2039, Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light Are Getting Next-Gen Updates
articles.summary: Metro 2039 is not too far away, launching on February 4, 2027. While that game will truly bring the franchise into the current generation, developer 4A Games is launching next-gen updates for the first two games.
articles.body:
Metro 2039 is not terribly far away now, launching on February 4, 2027. While that game will truly bring the franchise to current generation consoles, developer 4A Games is launching next-gen updates for the first two games.

Both Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light were incredible tech showcases for their time, but they haven't exactly aged gracefully. Despite getting an intial remaster all the way back in 2014, Metro 2033 doesn't play super well with modern hardware, and I've needed to tweak it every time I've gone back to play it. Luckily, these next-gen updates should bring some long-needed bug fixes to the game.

The update will look different on console and on PC. For PS5 and Xbox Series X , the Metro games will run at either native 4K at 60 fps or an upscaled 4K at 120 fps, with PSSR on PS5 Pro and traditional temporal upscaling on the Xbox consoles. Over on PC, though, the game will finally have DLSS support, along with some unnamed quality-of-life improvements.

4A Games hasn't shared a lot of details on the updates coming to Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light, but it does promise to share full patch notes ahead of its October 22 release on PC and October 29 release on consoles. Either way, as long as the games are more stable, I'm all in.

As a lifelong PC gamer, all three of the Metro games hold a special place in my heart, for all the torture they've put my graphics cards through in the past. Luckily, if you don't like putting your hardware through the wringer, it doesn't sound like 4A is going to add ray tracing or anything crazy to 2033 or Last Light, so they should be significantly easier to run at high settings than they were when they launched in 2010 and 2013.

We've already gone hands-on with Metro 2039 , and it seems like an incredible and brutal post-apocalyptic shooter — just like I'd want out of the franchise. The visuals we've seen so far look incredible too, so I can only imagine that it's going to stay true to its roots of pushing PC hardware to its limits. Although, it is launching in the middle of an ongoing RAM crisis, which is going to limit its already niche appeal a bit when the benchmarks start rolling out. Here's to hoping 4A Games finds a way to make a Metro game scalable at launch for once.

articles.title: How GTA 6's Jason and Lucia Have Evolved Since 2023 in Pictures
articles.summary: GTA 6 officially releases next month, so we're taking a look at how the game's two protagonists, Jason and Lucia, have evolved since their 2023 reveal.
articles.body:
GTA 6 officially releases next month, so we're taking a look at how the game's two protagonists, Jason and Lucia, have evolved since their 2023 reveal.

If there's one thing Rockstar has consistently managed to achieve, it's that its finished games often look better than the reveal trailers. That isn't the case for many game studios. In fact, a lot of games have been slammed for being downgraded between their reveals and launches. Watch Dogs, Cyberpunk 2077, and BioShock Infinite are all solid games, but they looked even better when they were initially revealed.

GTA 6 appears to have only visually improved over time, and that is most evident in the level of detail on protagonists Jason and Lucia. In 2023, we got our first official look at GTA 6 with the first trailer. There had been some leaks prior to this, but this was the first time Rockstar showed the game itself. The game looked stunning with gorgeous lighting effects, vivid colors, and realistic-looking characters. Rockstar would then go dark for a year and a half before re-revealing the game, and the graphical leap was absurdly impressive.

In Pictures: How GTA 6's Jason and Lucia Have Evolved Since 2023

Compared to the 2023 trailer, GTA 6's visuals have drastically changed. The overall art direction remained the same, but the level of detail presented in the character models changed massively during this period. In the first trailer, Lucia's skin looks less textured, more flat, and less nuanced. Her hair also doesn't move much; there's a bit of bounce to her ponytail, but it's more limited. She also has the same hairstyle throughout the entire trailer, outside of some loose strands of hair on the sides of her face in the opening shots.

Jason only gets a few seconds to shine, but he largely looks like a generic white guy with his shaved head and stubble. Trailer 2, however, provides a lot more depth. Both characters sport a variety of hairstyles, with Lucia rocking wavy hair and a golden dress. Jason's brown hair flows out of the back of his hat. His skin glistens after sweating in the Vice City heat, his veins outline his arms, and his facial hair appears to be somewhat uneven, with certain strands of hair poking out slightly further than others. These human imperfections are perfections in the world of a video game trying to emulate realistic people. The light also bounces off of their skin in a more natural way.

It's a clear showcase of not only the level of detail, but also the amount of customization the player will have. That mindset carried into the recent extended look for GTA 6. The visual leap wasn't as large as the one between trailer 1 and 2, but it does feel like a world of difference from trailer 1 itself. There's infinitely more customization options and Jason and Lucia are clearly at their final level of polish.

Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson recently stated that trailer 1 was a "mission statement" for the team, as the game wasn't "fully formed." It was a north star for the team to follow and something they could point to as a way of understanding the overall vision for the game. As a result, it makes sense that the game has only improved since then.

GTA 6 is just weeks away from release now and the finishing touches are being added to the game. The ESRB officially rated the game M for Mature this morning and Rockstar is starting to ramp up its marketing efforts with physical ads in places like Miami and New York. After years of waiting, GTA 6 will finally be here on November 19.
